hints: Think about what happens to the $\text{NH}_2$ and $\text{COOH}$ groups as pH changes, and at what pH the positive and negative charges exactly balance.
walkthrough:
Picture glycine changing with pH**
Remember glycine can gain $\text{H}^+$ in acid to become a cation and lose $\text{H}^+$ in alkali to become an anion. In between there is one special pH where it has both a $\text{NH}_3^+$ and a $\text{COO}^-$ at the same time, so the +1 and -1 cancel to zero net charge. That pH is the isoelectric point.
Final answer: The pH at which the amino acid has no overall charge / exists as a zwitterion with charges cancelling.

hints: Compare pH 4 with the isoelectric point 6.2 to decide if the solution is more acidic, then recall which groups pick up $\text{H}^+$ in acid.
walkthrough:
Decide if you add or remove protons**
The isoelectric point is 6.2, so pH 4 is more acidic, meaning excess $\text{H}^+$. Both basic sites will be protonated where possible. The amine becomes $\text{H}_3\overset{+}{\text{N}}-$ and the carboxylate $\text{COO}^-$ becomes $\text{COOH}$, giving the fully protonated cation $\text{H}_3\overset{+}{\text{N}}\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$.

hints: Look at reaction 1, glycine plus $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Br}$ to give a tertiary amine, and recall what solvent and heating method is needed for nucleophilic substitution by amines with haloalkanes.
walkthrough:
Recognise the alkylation**
The $\text{NH}_2$ group of glycine acts as a nucleophile attacking $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Br}$, replacing Br with ethyl groups twice to give $(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{NCH}_2\text{COOH}$. This nucleophilic substitution of a bromoalkane by an amine needs ethanol as solvent with heating under pressure, so you state ethanol and heat in a sealed tube.
Final answer: Ethanol and heat in a sealed tube OR ethanol and high pressure.

hints: Compare glycine $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{COOH}$ with hippuric acid $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CONHCH}_2\text{COOH}$ and ask what benzoyl reagent can attach $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CO}-$ to nitrogen at room temperature.
walkthrough:
Spot the new amide link**
Hippuric acid has a $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CO-NH}-$ group where glycine had $\text{H}_2\text{N}-$. You need to form an amide from an amine, and carboxylic acids are too unreactive. The reactive acylating agent is benzoyl chloride, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl}$.
Final answer: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl}$ / benzoyl chloride.

hints: Recall what excess $\text{LiAlH}_4$ does separately to a carboxylic acid group and to an amide group.
Apply both changes to hippuric acid $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CONHCH}_2\text{COOH}$ while leaving the benzene ring untouched.
walkthrough:
Reduce the acid end**
Excess $\text{LiAlH}_4$ is a powerful reducing agent. It reduces the carboxylic acid $-\text{COOH}$ all the way to a primary alcohol $-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$. So $-\text{NHCH}_2\text{COOH}$ becomes $-\text{NHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$.

Reduce the amide link**
The same reagent also reduces the amide carbonyl $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CONH}-$ to $\text{CH}_2$, giving an amine $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{NH}-$. Put both together with the unchanged phenyl ring to get $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{NHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ as U.

hints: Remember a dipeptide forms by condensation between $\text{COOH}$ of one amino acid and $\text{NH}_2$ of the other with loss of water, giving a fully displayed $-\text{CO-NH}-$ link.
Think about the two possible orders using phenylalanine R $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}(\text{CH}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5)\text{COOH}$ and glycine $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{COOH}$.
walkthrough:
Build the first order**
If phenylalanine provides the $\text{COOH}$ and glycine provides the $\text{NH}_2$, you join them to get $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CONHCH}(\text{CH}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5)\text{COOH}$, which can be written as $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}(\text{CH}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5)\text{CONHCH}_2\text{COOH}$ depending on left to right order. Show the $-\text{C}(=\text{O})-\text{N}(\text{H})-$ atoms explicitly.

Build the reverse order**
If glycine provides the $\text{COOH}$ and phenylalanine provides the $\text{NH}_2$, you get the isomer $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CONHCH}(\text{CH}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5)\text{COOH}$ reversed, i.e. $\text{HOOCCH}(\text{CH}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5)\text{NHCOCH}_2\text{NH}_2$. These two are structural isomers S and T.

Final answer: S and T are: $\text{HOOCCH}(\text{CH}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5)\text{NHCOCH}_2\text{NH}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}(\text{CH}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5)\text{CONHCH}_2\text{COOH}$ with peptide bond $\text{CO-NH}$ fully displayed.

hints: Think about where the nitrogen lone pair is in an amine $\text{R-NH}_2$ compared to an amide $\text{R-CONH}_2$ next to a $\text{C=O}$ group.
Link availability of that lone pair to accept $\text{H}^+$ with strength as a base.
walkthrough:
Locate the lone pair**
In an amine the lone pair sits localised on nitrogen, ready to form a dative bond to $\text{H}^+$. In an amide $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CONH}_2$ that same lone pair overlaps with the pi system of the adjacent $\text{C=O}$, it is delocalised over N, C and O.

Link to basicity**
A base works by donating its lone pair to $\text{H}^+$. Because the amide lone pair is already tied up in delocalisation, electron density on N is lower and it is much less available to accept $\text{H}^+$. Hence benzamide is a very weak base and a poor nucleophile.

Final answer: In amides the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised with the C=O / overlapped with the carbonyl pi system.
The lone pair is less available for donation / to accept $\text{H}^+$, so amides are weaker bases.

hints: Recall that lower $pK_a$ means stronger acid, so decide which acid is stronger from 2.86 versus 4.76.
Consider how the electronegative Cl atom pulls electrons through sigma bonds and what this does to the O-H bond and to the stability of the $\text{RCOO}^-$ anion.
walkthrough:
Translate pKa**
Lower $pK_a$ means larger $K_a$ and stronger acid. So chloroethanoic acid ($pK_a$ 2.86) is significantly stronger than ethanoic acid ($pK_a$ 4.76).

Explain with the -I effect**
Chlorine is highly electronegative and withdraws electron density through the sigma bonds. This pulls charge away from the $\text{COO}$ group, weakening the O-H bond so $\text{H}^+$ is lost more easily, and it disperses the negative charge on the resulting $\text{ClCH}_2\text{COO}^-$ anion, stabilising it relative to $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$. A more stable conjugate base means a stronger acid.

Final answer: Chloroethanoic acid is a stronger acid than ethanoic acid.
The Cl has an electron withdrawing inductive (-I) effect which weakens the O-H bond / stabilises the carboxylate anion.

hints: Use Table 6.1 to match each environment: a is $\text{RCOOH}$, b is aromatic H, c is $\text{CH}_2$ next to Ar, d is $\text{CH}_2$ next to N.
Recall that protons on O or N next to carbon do not normally split neighbours in simple analysis, focus on neighbouring C-H protons for splitting.
Apply the n+1 rule: a $\text{CH}_2$ next to one $\text{CH}_2$ (2 equivalent H) gives a triplet.
Remember that $\text{COOH}$ and $\text{NH}_2$ protons with no C-H neighbours appear as singlets, while aromatic protons with non equivalent neighbours appear as a multiplet.
walkthrough:
Assign chemical shifts from Table 6.1**
Proton a is the carboxylic acid $\text{HOOC}-$, Table gives 9.0-13.0. Proton b is aromatic $\text{H-Ar}$, Table gives 6.0-9.0. Proton c is $\text{CH}_2$ next to aromatic ring $\text{CH}_2\text{-Ar}$, Table gives 2.3-3.0. Proton d is $\text{CH}_2$ next to electronegative N $\text{CH}_2\text{-N}$, Table gives 3.2-4.0. Proton e is alkyl amine $\text{R-NH}_2$, Table gives 1.0-5.0.

Predict splitting with n+1**
Proton a ($\text{COOH}$) has no adjacent C-H, so singlet. Proton b covers four aromatic H in two pairs of environments that couple to each other, so multiplet (given). Proton c ($\text{Ar-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2$) is next to 2 H on d, so 2+1 = triplet. Proton d ($\text{CH}_2\text{-NH}_2$ next to c) is next to 2 H on c, so triplet. Proton e ($\text{NH}_2$) has no C-H splitting counted here, so singlet.

Assemble the table**
Put shifts and splittings together: a singlet at 9.0-13.0, b multiplet at 6.0-9.0, c triplet at 2.3-3.0, d triplet at 3.2-4.0, e singlet at 1.0-5.0. This uses both shift and neighbour logic, not just memorising numbers.
Final answer: a: $\delta$ 9.0-13.0, singlet; b: $\delta$ 6.0-9.0, multiplet; c: $\delta$ 2.3-3.0, triplet; d: $\delta$ 3.2-4.0, triplet; e: $\delta$ 1.0-5.0, singlet.

hints: Recall which protons exchange with $\text{D}_2\text{O}$ (O-H and N-H) and disappear, versus C-H protons on the ring and chain which remain.
walkthrough:
Sort labile from non labile**
Proton a is $\text{O-H}$ of the acid and proton e is $\text{N-H}$ of the amine, both are labile and exchange with deuterium to give O-D and N-D, so their $^1\text{H}$ peaks vanish. Protons b (aromatic C-H), c ($\text{CH}_2$) and d ($\text{CH}_2$) are bonded to carbon, they cannot exchange, so they stay visible in $\text{D}_2\text{O}$.
Final answer: Protons b, c, d remain (ticks); protons a and e absent (exchange with $\text{D}_2\text{O}$).
